overview.text: Thomas Alva Edison (1847–1931) was an American inventor and businessman whose work helped turn new technologies into industries. At his Menlo Park laboratory, he developed the phonograph, which could both record and replay sound, and pursued electric lighting—not by originating the idea of electric light, but by making an incandescent lamp and a practical lighting-and-power system. He later built a large research operation in West Orange. Edison’s motion-picture work also depended on collaborators, especially William K. L. Dickson: their Kinetograph camera and Kinetoscope viewer helped launch early movies, produced at the Black Maria studio. His legacy is best understood as invention combined with development, manufacturing, and commercialization.

key_facts.text: Edison was born in Milan, Ohio, in 1847, and died in West Orange, New Jersey, in 1931.
His 1877 phonograph used a stylus and tinfoil to record sound and could play the recording back.
Electric lighting was not a new idea; Edison’s notable achievement was developing a practical incandescent lamp and the system needed to supply light and power.
Edison’s motion-picture work included the Kinetograph camera and Kinetoscope viewer; associate William K. L. Dickson played a key role in developing the equipment.
The Black Maria, a studio at Edison’s West Orange complex, produced short films featuring popular variety acts.
